title: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
body:
Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , the AWS SDKs , and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker. How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged. From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region. The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023 . The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/ , so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest
sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm

aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator . It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 , so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR , so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000 . curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started
make_bucket: local-getting-started

$ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt

$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/
upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
      are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
      "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
      {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
      back with get-item.

$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
    --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'

$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java . For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust . You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
    AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
    ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
    let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest())
        .http_client(emulator.http_client())
        .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1"))
        .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider())
        .load()
        .await;
    let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

    ddb.create_table()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .attribute_definitions(
            AttributeDefinition::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S)
                .build().unwrap())
        .key_schema(
            KeySchemaElement::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash)
                .build().unwrap())
        .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest)
        .send().await.unwrap();

    ddb.put_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();

    let got = ddb.get_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
} When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline , and AWS CodeCommit , so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, see the AWS Emulator documentation.

It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023 . The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/ , so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest
sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm

aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator . It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 , so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR , so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000 . curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started
make_bucket: local-getting-started

$ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt

$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/
upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
      are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
      "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
      {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
      back with get-item.

$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
    --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'

$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java . For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust . You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
    AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
    ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
    let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest())
        .http_client(emulator.http_client())
        .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1"))
        .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider())
        .load()
        .await;
    let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

    ddb.create_table()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .attribute_definitions(
            AttributeDefinition::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S)
                .build().unwrap())
        .key_schema(
            KeySchemaElement::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash)
                .build().unwrap())
        .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest)
        .send().await.unwrap();

    ddb.put_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();

    let got = ddb.get_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
} When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline , and AWS CodeCommit , so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, see the AWS Emulator documentation.

title: Built on Googlebook: Play Henry Cavill’s video game to support Movember
body: Built on Googlebook: Play Henry Cavill’s video game to support Movember Nov 11, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link “Mustache Protocol” is live. See how the 16-bit adventure came together on Googlebook, and help us drive awareness for men’s health. Menaka Shroff (MK) Vice President, Marketing, Global Android Ecosystem Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We collaborated with Henry Cavill to create Mustache Protocol, a new 16-bit video game built entirely on Googlebook. You can play this retro-style game in your browser to support men’s health, as we will donate $11 to Movember for every play through November 30. Visit googlebook.com/henry to start your quest, watch the behind-the-scenes episodes, and contribute to this important cause. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Menaka Shroff, Vice President of Marketing, announces that Henry Cavill built a game called Mustache Protocol. You can play this retro-style game on your desktop or mobile device using simple arcade controls. We will donate 11 dollars to Movember for every game played until the end of November. Your participation supports awareness for men's mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We teamed up with Henry Cavill to create a retro video game called Mustache Protocol using our Googlebook tools. You can play this game in your browser to help us support Movember. For every game you play through November 30, we will donate $11 to men’s health causes, up to a total of $500,000. Visit our site to start playing, save the mustaches, and contribute to this important mission. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Henry Cavill teamed up with Google to build “Mustache Protocol,” a 16-bit video game, on his Googlebook. Over the past few weeks, we’ve watched Henry’s creative process unfold. In the first episode of our behind-the-scenes series, he designed a handlebar-mustachioed hero using Magic Pointer and Quick Access . In the second episode, he used Rambler to create superpowers and health boosts. Today, we’re sharing the final episode — and the game is officially ready for you to play. Watch the episode In the third episode of the series, Henry puts the finishing touches on his game. Every great game needs a theme song, and the finale shows how with a little help from Googlebook, Henry brought the game’s audio together. Let’s dive in: Continue On: Henry previewed a smooth, ’70s-style track on his Android phone, then used Continue On to move the music to his Googlebook desktop without interrupting his flow. Rambler and BandLab: After Henry plugged in a drum pad to add custom musical beats using BandLab and recorded sultry baritone vocals, Rambler turned his voice commands into clean prompts to drop the track and sound effects into the game. Antigravity: Using Antigravity , the next-gen agentic platform built into Googlebook, Henry stitched together the final visuals, level layouts, and interactive elements — the last steps in taking the game from an idea to a live, playable build. Play “Mustache Protocol” and support Movember “Mustache Protocol” is ready for you to play . The retro-style game sends players on an epic quest across three levels to stop a rogue CGI agent from erasing every mustache on the planet. It is, as Henry told us, "super serious." You can play directly in your web browser or on your desktop or mobile device using simple arcade controls to move, jump, and swing your mustache-comb sword. To make the game uniquely his, Henry packed each level with hilarious power-ups and Easter eggs. See if you can spot all of them. Henry steps up as the mustachioed hero to save the world’s mustaches this Movember. Keep an eye out for cameos from Henry's beloved dogs, Kal and Baggins. Power up with a “tank attack” and watch Henry celebrate with a dance. Power up with an “arm reload” to boost your attack power before a big fight. Quick tip for playing: an overview of keyboard controls. In honor of Movember , your gameplay supports men’s health. From November 11 to 30, for every game played, Google will donate $11 to Movember, up to $500,000. Every play helps drive awareness and funding for men’s mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer. So fire up your browser and help us save the world’s mustaches. Head to googlebook.com/henry to play “Mustache Protocol,” watch all three episodes, and join the movement. Get the latest news from Google in your inbox Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. Done. Just one step more. Check your inbox to confirm your subscription. You can also subscribe with a different email address . Your information will be used in accordance with Google's privacy policy. You may opt out at any time. Posted in:

title: Get certified as a Google Cloud Professional Agentic Architect.
body: Get certified as a Google Cloud Professional Agentic Architect. Gary Eimerman Managing Director, Google GTM Learning Practice Lead Nov 11, 2026 Today we announced Google Cloud's new Professional Agentic Architect certification: an industry-recognized certification that proves you can deploy secure, enterprise-grade agents that automate multi-step and multi-app workflows. This hybrid certification has two parts: a proctored multiple-choice exam assessing foundational knowledge in agentic architecture, and Google Skills labs to evaluate real-world, hands-on practical experience. Over the past four months, Google Cloud has trained thousands of Google Cloud forward deployed engineers and Google Cloud partners on this advanced curriculum. This certification is now available for technical professionals like developers, cloud architects, and engineers who architect, build, and deploy agents on Google Cloud. Our research shows more than 80% of Google Cloud certified individuals say the credential opens doors to new career opportunities and accelerates their path to promotion. Furthermore, 82% of individuals say certifications from Google Cloud help them earn higher salaries 1 . Start your preparation at no cost today. Sign up for Gemini Agent Ready to claim 35 free monthly learning credits and gain access to our hands-on labs and agentic courses. Learn more on our Google Cloud blog .

title: Google Cloud leaders share what to expect in cybersecurity for 2027.
body: Google Cloud leaders share what to expect in cybersecurity for 2027. Nov 11, 2026 As enterprise software shifts from static applications to autonomous agents managing core operations, cybersecurity is facing a fundamental transformation. In our Security 2027 analysis, leaders from across Google, Google Cloud, and Mandiant break down the critical trends shaping the next era of defense. Key priorities for 2027 include : Protecting decision integrity: Ensuring every consequential autonomous action is secure and 100% explainable Moving "Beyond Zero": Never blindly trusting any AI tool, and having visibility into what they can access and what they are doing Winning with ground truth: Using multi-model AI ensembles to correlate internal context and remediate risks at machine speed before attackers can piece them together Watch the Security 2027 overview video below, and read the full executive perspective on the Google Cloud Blog .

Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer For millions of people, the daily commute averages about an hour behind the wheel. While voice assistants have long been great for quick tasks like playing a playlist or getting directions home, all that quiet time on the road is also an opportunity to catch up, prepare for what’s ahead, or simply think out loud. Following our rollout on Android Auto and cars with Google built-in , today we’re bringing the Gemini app directly to Apple CarPlay. Now, iOS users can have natural, free-flowing conversations with Gemini Live right from their car’s display — hands-free, so you can get more done while keeping your hands on the wheel and your eyes on the road. Pick up where you left off — or start a fresh conversation We designed Gemini on CarPlay to work like a conversational driving companion that minimizes distraction. When you tap the Gemini app icon on your CarPlay screen or side rail, you can easily pick up where you left off with a recent chat or start a fresh conversation. You can talk back and forth with Gemini at your own pace — interrupting to add a detail, changing the subject, or pausing when you need to focus on an exit. Make the most of your drive Whether you’re commuting or setting out on a road trip, Gemini on CarPlay helps you be more productive during your ride. Here are a few ways to make the most of your drive: Get ready for the day ahead: Use your morning commute to see what's coming up and walk into your first meeting prepared. Ask Gemini what's on your calendar, when you need to leave for your next appointment, or talk through what you want to say before you arrive. Try saying: "What does my day look like?" or "Help me prep for my 10am with the design team." Talk through your inbox: Because Gemini connects with your Google Workspace apps like Gmail and Google Calendar, you can ask for your daily brief 1 , catch up on unread emails, get quick summaries of long email threads, and talk through a quick reply using just your voice. Try saying: “Give me my daily brief for today,” or “Catch me up on my unread emails and summarize Sarah’s Q4 budget thread.” Explore local spots and landmarks: Ask Gemini for recommendations in the area you’re heading to, from a quick place to grab lunch to the backstory on a local landmark. Try saying: “What’s a quick lunch spot in downtown Austin that’s easy to get in and out of?” Brainstorm, rehearse, and learn out loud: A quiet car cabin is one of the best places to think out loud. Use Gemini Live as a sounding board to practice an upcoming presentation, prepare for a tough conversation, or break down a complex topic you’ve been curious about. Try saying: “Let’s roleplay my Q4 pitch — act as a skeptical VP and challenge my strategy,” or “Break down how solid-state EV batteries work in simple terms.” And because your CarPlay conversations sync automatically with the Gemini app on your iPhone, every summary, note, and brainstorm is waiting in your chat history the moment you park. Get started today Gemini on Apple CarPlay is rolling out globally starting today to all Gemini users on iOS across every supported Gemini Live language. To get started, make sure you’ve updated to the latest version of the Gemini app on your iPhone, enabled microphone permissions, and used Gemini Live on your phone at least once. The next time you connect your phone to your car, tap the Gemini icon on your CarPlay display, then start a new conversation or pick up a recent one. title: Google’s ongoing commitment to the veteran community
body: Google’s ongoing commitment to the veteran community Nov 11, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Google invests in career pathways and grassroots support to help veterans and military spouses successfully transition and thrive at every stage of their civilian lives. Michael Reeves Global co-lead, Google Veterans Network, Employee Resource Group Ronnie Ryder Global co-lead, Google Veterans Network, Employee Resource Group Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary Michael Reeves and Ronnie Ryder share how Google supports veterans through career training and community partnerships. Our Google Launchpad for Veterans program provides service members with cloud and generative AI skill training. We offer no-cost scholarships and digital certificates to help veterans and military spouses find civilian jobs. Google.org supports organizations that help veterans build long-term careers in skilled trades and technical fields. Our teams use AI and 3D technology to connect deployed service members with their families globally. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. As co-leads of the Google Veterans Network (VetNet) Employee Resource Group, we see daily how veterans’ skills translate into high-impact workforce leadership. Through deep collaborations with global non-profits, industry partners, and our own product teams, Google is continuing to invest in career pathways and grassroots support to help veterans and military spouses successfully transition and thrive at every stage of their civilian lives. Expanding skills and career pathways A central part of our efforts is providing veterans with career resources and trainings in the latest tech skills. Here’s what we’re doing: Google Launchpad for Veterans : Now in its third year, this program helps active-duty personnel, transitioning service members, and veterans build practical cloud and generative AI skills, preparing them for credentials like the Generative AI Leader certification. Certifications — available at no cost through this program — are known to help open up career opportunities. In fact, 92% of Google Skills learners say Google Cloud credentials (certifications, skill badges) help them get in-demand jobs faster. 1 Veterans Career Week : Hosted alongside Grow with Google, our flagship initiative expanded internationally this year programming across the U.S., Europe, and Asia-Pacific, reaching over 6,000 participants. At our hands-on Grow with Google workshops, veterans and military families used tools like Career Dreamer, which translates their military experience into civilian resumes. They also received no-cost scholarships for digital and AI training, including the Google AI Professional Certificate . Today, one in ten Google Career Certificate graduates comes from the military community. National Veterans Small Business Week : Grow with Google teamed up with American Corporate Partners (ACP) and Blue Star Families to deliver hands-on AI training during our third annual National Veterans Small Business Week livestream. Attendees learned practical AI skills and gained insights from a veteran-owned small business. Skilled Trades Initiative : Google.org is supporting Hiring Our Heroes, Home Builders Institute, and Student Veterans of America to help 25,000 veterans and military family members build long-term careers in skilled trades. This builds upon prior funding to support student veterans nationwide with broad career readiness programming, including access to Google Career Certificates and Google AI Professional Certificate. Public Sector Enablement : Working alongside partners like Carahsoft, Google Cloud has trained more than 40,000 public sector personnel, including active duty service members and reservists, equipping our military with the hands-on expertise to safely architect what’s next. Investing in community organizations This year’s Google Veteran Impact Awards delivered $500,000 in new funding across four high-impact organizations. Nominated by VetNet Googlers with deep personal ties to their work, these nonprofits represent the groups our veteran community trusts, champions, and volunteers for: FourBlock : Leads employer-hosted transition programs, taught directly by corporate leaders at active workplaces, for veterans to build direct networks and translate their military experience using an AI-enabled platform. Blue Star Families : Serves as the nation’s largest military and veteran family support organization, strengthening families through trusted resources, community partnerships, and scam-prevention education. The Von Terra Project : Empowers veterans transitioning to advanced technical careers through offerings like its comprehensive cybersecurity certification program, which features learning resources, fully funded exam vouchers, and one-on-one industry mentorship. The Job Forum : Facilitates volunteer-led advising where experienced executives and hiring professionals help veterans and spouses translate skills and prepare for interviews. Spotlighting veterans through our products Across Google's products and platforms, we are celebrating and connecting the military community: Google Beam and USO: In partnership with the USO, we’re expanding HP Dimension with Google Beam to 20 locations globally. Powered by AI and 3D technology, Beam provides true-to-life video communication that lets deployed service members and their families feel like they are stepping into the same space. Watch our docuseries connecting four soldiers in Poland with their families in Texas; goo.gle/uso-beam Google Doodle: Our annual Veterans Day Doodle recognizes service, dedication, and courage with the achievement medals representing the six branches of service. These merit-based awards, which honor exceptional teamwork or technical achievements, often represent a junior officer’s, warrant officer’s, or enlisted service member's first individual award for superior performance of their duties and are an important point of pride in veteran life. Camaraderie and purpose don’t end when service members hang up their uniforms. For the thousands of military families transitioning to civilian life each year, that shared sense of mission endures — and at Google, we recognize that the resilience, adaptability, and teamwork forged in service are invaluable assets to our teams. To our veterans, service members, and military families: thank you for your service and leadership. title: Try Tabletop: Customizable, collaborative spaces for groups to plan, play and do more together.
body: Try Tabletop: Customizable, collaborative spaces for groups to plan, play and do more together. Roman Nurik Design & Engineering Lead, Google Labs Nov 11, 2026 Whether you’re planning a family trip, running a rec league or hosting a potluck, coordinating as a group is easier when everyone can pitch in, build and decide together in one place. Today, we’re introducing Tabletop , a new Google Labs experiment built for real-time collaboration. Just add in your links, files, and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters, and tournament brackets. Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time, like in a Google Doc. Tabletop is rolling out in the U.S. (18+) via waitlist. Pull up a chair and sign up at labs.google/tabletop .

body: Experience the art and legacy of Dr. Esther Mahlangu Nov 11, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Discover Google Arts & Culture's online retrospective of the South African artist, which features more than 45 curated stories, virtual tours, and her early memories brought to life with AI. This collection features over 45 stories, archival materials, and AI-generated recreations of her early life to preserve Ndebele heritage for a global audience. Dr. Nontobeko Ntombela presents the first online retrospective of artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu on Google Arts & Culture. You can explore over 45 stories, rare archival materials, and murals documenting her life and artistic legacy. We used artificial intelligence to recreate undocumented memories from her early years before her first recorded works. This project preserves Ndebele culture by combining historical research with new video technology for a global audience. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are celebrating artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu with a new online retrospective on Google Arts & Culture. Because some of her early history was missing, we used artificial intelligence to recreate her childhood memories based on her own stories. You can now explore over 45 exhibitions, view her murals, and learn about Ndebele culture from anywhere in the world. This project preserves her artistic legacy for you and future generations to enjoy. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Today we’re sharing the first online retrospective of artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu on Google Arts & Culture, honoring her pioneering spirit on her 91st birthday. More than 45 stories and a rich archive covering her art , life , and legacy are now accessible to a global audience. For many years, I have worked closely with Esther and her family. It’s a relationship built on years of research and a deep admiration for her as both an artist and a person. It was out of this long-standing connection that the vision for “‘ Then I Knew I Was Good at Painting’: Esther Mahlangu, a Retrospective ,” was born. My goal has always been to present a comprehensive exploration of her life and work, contributing to my long-standing research on South African women artists who have made an impact on the arts since the early 20th century. Through my research, I gathered a rich collection of her work, including large-scale murals , intimate pieces , and rare archival materials . But the archives didn’t include anything from her life before 1980, so crucial pieces of her history were missing. This void challenged us to find new ways to tell her full story. A collaboration session with Esther Mahlangu, Nontobeko Ntombela, and the Google team. In collaboration with Google Arts & Culture, we used AI to visually recreate Esther’s undocumented memories . The process brought us closer to her work and prompted further recollections from Esther herself. This project brought our curatorial and archival work together with the technical expertise of Google DeepMind and Google Arts & Culture Lab, alongside research and design studio Domestic Data Streamers’ synthetic memories initiative. Through a series of workshops and interviews , we were able to document a missing period of Mam' Esther's history, from when she started painting at age 10 until her first documented works in 1980. These stories — such as the moment she discovered her talent for painting as a 10-year-old using feathers instead of a brush — became the source material for our work. Following the methodology from the synthetic memories initiative and using archival material, the team generated still images based on Esther’s memories. They then used Veo to turn the images into videos that brought Esther's early days to life. The stories also contribute to the online archive of Esther’s life on Google Arts & Culture. More than 45 exhibitions , curated in collaboration with Art of Contemporary Africa, Iziko Museums of South Africa, the British Museum, the Jean Pigozzi Collection, the National Museum of Women in the Arts, and Serpentine, tell the story of how she came to be known in the world, through her artwork , archives, Street View , and more. Portrait of Esther Mahlangu taken at Botshabelo, c. 1980-1991; Art of Contemporary Africa | Source Esther Mahlangu: Untitled, 2014; Art of Contemporary Africa | Source The Esther Mahlangu Art Studio at the Esther Mahlangu Homestead, 2025; Art of Contemporary Africa | Source Installation of the Esther Mahlangu retrospective at Iziko South African National Gallery, 2024; Art of Contemporary Africa | Source Esther Mahlangu: Ndebele Abstract, 2019; Art of Contemporary Africa, courtesy of the Larry Warsh Collection | Source This project demonstrates a new way to approach the preservation of cultural heritage, with technology that’s guided at every step by a respect for personal memory and historical accuracy. It is my hope that this retrospective cements Esther’s place as a pivotal voice in global contemporary art, invites audiences to reimagine the possibilities of her archive, and ensures her story and her artistic vision can inspire generations to come. title: Remarks from Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent at the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations Gala
body: November 11, 2026 As prepared for delivery. Thank you, Evan [Greenberg], for that introduction, and for the invitation to be here. It gives me great pleasure to join you on this occasion. More than as representatives of the world’s largest economies, we meet tonight as stewards of one of this century’s most consequential relationships. Of course, when this Committee was formed in 1966, the Pacific was only the most visible distance between the United States and China. Formal diplomatic ties were still over a decade away. Our governments rarely spoke. And our people, likewise, rarely met. But a “small, loosely cohesive” band of China watchers believed that distance was reason to know more, not less. And so, they set out to understand China more deeply and to engage with it more seriously. They could not anticipate where exactly the relationship would lead, only that it would matter. The founders of this Committee set for themselves the ambitious task of reaching all segments of society—“from the layman, through the specialist, to the policy maker”—and “forging enduring links” between them. Tonight, sixty years later, take one look around this room, and you can see how fully their ambition has been realized. The United States and China represent different systems. Our national interests often diverge. But the links that you have built now bind generations and cultures together. They reach public servants and private citizens. Scholars who are bringing new ideas to light and entrepreneurs who are putting new ideas into practice. On both sides of the Pacific, people understand each other better because the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations brought them together. So, before I go any further, let me recognize two men who embody the best of this work. Steve Orlins has devoted much of his professional life to the U.S.-China relationship. He was part of the team that established diplomatic relations in the 1970s and then spent decades strengthening the ties that sustain them. Steve, you leave behind a legacy of great consequence, for which I offer my sincere thanks and congratulations. I am also pleased to acknowledge our second honoree. If Steve Orlins has shaped the history of our engagement with China, Stephen Schwarzman has made a transformative investment in its future. By founding the Schwarzman Scholars program, he has carried forward the conviction that animates this Committee. Relationships between nations are built on relationships between people. Steve, a new generation of leaders will be better prepared to navigate the U.S.-China relationship because you have given them the chance to understand it—and one another—more deeply. Congratulations. Now, while this Committee has supported bilateral relations for decades, the truth is that the ties between us span centuries. In fact, our relationship with China is nearly as old as the republic itself. In the winter of 1784, before we had a president—before we even had a constitution—an American ship, the Empress of China, departed New York Harbor and turned her bow toward the Pearl River. The vessel carried American crew and cargo, and with them, the confidence of a young country that had won its independence and was already reaching for a place among the great trading nations of the world. Major Samuel Shaw, who later served as the first American consul to China, recalled that upon the ship’s arrival, the Chinese people “were highly pleased at the prospect of so considerable a market for the productions of theirs.” Two nations, once separated by great distance, were drawn together by the possibilities of exchange. So before Washington and Beijing had ambassadors, we had merchants. Before our envoys learned how to engage, our people had already discovered how to do business. And before diplomacy gave this relationship its shape, the flow of goods gave it its force. Shaw celebrated that flow of commerce in both directions. And he was clear about the terms on which that commerce should proceed: “in all cases equal.” Even then, Americans expected a fair footing. Nearly two and a half centuries have passed since the Empress made her maiden voyage. What began with a single American ship bound for Canton—what began with the trading of ginseng for porcelain, tea, and silk—has matured into a vast trading network between the world’s two largest economies. Of course, the world that Samuel Shaw inhabited has long receded into history. But the instinct that carried him across an ocean endures. Americans still seek now what we sought then, which is to pursue opportunity wherever it lies, and to insist on fairness wherever we compete. Trade must advance the interests of both parties without diminishing the sovereignty of either. And it is precisely in that spirit that President Trump has approached our relationship with China. Today, U.S.-China relations are defined by the relationship between our two leaders. From the time of his first election, President Trump has, in his own words, “forged a friendship [with President Xi] built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people.” That friendship has brought unprecedented direct engagement between the leaders of our two nations, which I try to extend to the working level. Of course, in May, President Trump traveled to Beijing. In September, President Xi came to Washington. And next week, I will join President Trump in Shenzhen, where the two leaders will meet before a fourth encounter in Miami. These meetings are historic in their frequency. Never before have our leaders engaged face-to-face so often in a single year. But more significant is the understanding they are helping to establish. President Trump and President Xi agree that the United States and China should build a constructive relationship on the basis of balance and reciprocity. And they’ve chartered two new institutions in service of those objectives. Under the Board of Trade, we reached consensus to identify more favorable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. The board also launched a working group to address trade barriers in the agricultural sector. And previously, China agreed to import at least 25 million metric tons of soybeans and 10 million metric tons of coal from the United States over the next two years. The Board of Investment, meanwhile, provides a structured forum for commercially meaningful issues, like market access for American companies and increased predictability for Chinese companies. And these initiatives are part of our broader work to advance a fair and reciprocal relationship with China. They give practical expression to the principle at the core of President Trump’s agenda, which is to measure the success of American engagement abroad by what it delivers here at home. By how it advances the prosperity of our people. Strengthens the resilience of our economy. And safeguards the security of our nation. Of course, the U.S. trade imbalance with China has long been a source of friction. And unlike a political class that tolerated China’s practices, President Trump has taken decisive steps to address them. Let me state firmly and unequivocally tonight that as we work toward a more balanced relationship, our objective is to de-risk, not to decouple. For decades, the American economy has grown too dependent on foreign supply, while China’s has become increasingly reliant on foreign demand. In other words, the United States must produce more of what we consume, while China must consume more of what it produces. Working together, we can strengthen both of our economies without perpetuating the imbalances between them. As Ray Dalio would say, we should have a big, beautiful rebalancing. So, as this President returns the American people to the center of American policy, let me be clear that our renewed emphasis on economic strength does not reflect hostility toward our trading partnerships. On the contrary, we are recovering the purpose that makes each of them worthwhile. After decades of imbalance, we are restoring a spirit of reciprocity for the benefit of both of our peoples. Now, as we work together to address the great questions of the last century, we must also summon the resolve to answer those of the next. In the final months of his life, Henry Kissinger was preoccupied with the challenges of a world he would not live to see. Even at the age of 100, his gaze, characteristically, was fixed on the future. On his last trip, he met with President Xi in Beijing to discuss deeper collaboration. Kissinger had come to believe that the advent of superintelligence could represent a novel class of strategic danger. And he recognized that the obligation of great nations, even—and perhaps especially—those with profound differences, is to find common purpose. So, at President Trump’s direction, we have begun that important work by establishing a new dialogue with China on SI, designed to guard against shared risks and prevent a misunderstanding between our two systems. We also expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology. Finally, we are establishing a direct channel to ensure that either nation can promptly alert the other to serious incidents involving its SI models. As SI advances, so will the need to engage in new areas of risk management—and to demonstrate how two nations can reconcile the demands of competition with the responsibilities of leadership. As we do so, we should harbor no illusions about the differences between the United States and China. As I stated earlier, our interests will not always coincide. And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge. Those early China watchers of the 1960s understood that the differences between our nations were too profound to ignore. But they also knew that the specter of our estrangement was too great to accept. Generations of leaders have demonstrated their faith in the value of this relationship, dating back to when those enterprising merchants aboard the Empress of China returned to New York Harbor. So I will take as my final words tonight those of Samuel Shaw, who, after a fourteen-month voyage, heralded “that a communication is thus happily opened between us and the Eastern Extreme of the Globe.” The patriots of 1784 opened that passage through commerce. The statesmen of the 1970s widened it through diplomacy. And for six decades, the men and women of this Committee have sustained it through the patient work of bringing our people together. Under President Trump, the United States will carry that work into a new era. We will enlarge the prospects for prosperity on both sides of the Pacific. And, secure in our own strength and unwavering commitment to the American people, we will honor those who first forged this relationship by renewing our resolve to strengthen it. Thank you and congratulations. ###

title: Bowman, The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy
body:

Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 10, 2026 The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman At the C. Peter McColough Series on International Economics Council on Foreign Relations, Washington, D.C. Share Watch Live Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman presented identical remarks at a subsequent event held by Unleash Prosperity Now on the same day. Good afternoon. It is a pleasure to join you today at the Council on Foreign Relations to discuss my outlook for the U.S. economy. 1 Economic growth has gained momentum this year, driven by robust investment demand and solid consumer spending, and the labor market now appears to have stabilized. These outcomes suggest that the policy rate cuts toward the end of last year helped to address some labor market weakness. We are experiencing rapid technological change and ongoing geopolitical tensions, while inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening. Despite these challenges, increased investment in and use of artificial intelligence (AI), or super intelligence, are boosting economic growth and productivity and American families appear to be resilient. The Federal Reserve's monetary policy goals are to achieve maximum employment and price stability. While the labor market has improved more than I expected this year, our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed. Therefore, bringing inflation down remains a priority. I am also monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices, and how they influence the risks to achieving our mandates. Consistent with my views following our September FOMC meeting, I continue to focus on interpreting the underlying trends in the economy and the evolution of financial conditions. 2 In my remarks today, I will review our most recent FOMC policy meeting and discuss current economic conditions and my near-term outlook for the economy. I will then turn to recent developments in energy markets and the AI buildout and will conclude with my thoughts on the appropriate path of monetary policy. Update on the Most Recent FOMC Meeting At last month's FOMC meeting, I joined my colleagues to support holding the federal funds rate target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent. This approach was consistent with my view that further changes in the policy rate should wait until we had a better understanding of how conditions would evolve and how the recent rate increase would influence the underlying trends in the economy. Maintaining the policy stance at the October meeting allowed us to assess the incoming data. While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated. It is also important to gain greater clarity on the effect of recent market volatility on financial conditions. Economic and Financial Conditions U.S. economic growth has stepped up this year. After rising a solid 2.4 percent during the first half of the year, real gross domestic product (GDP) likely increased at an even stronger pace of more than 3 percent in the third quarter, well above last year's 2 percent pace. 3 Economic growth has been supported by robust increases in AI-related capital expenditures and solid consumer spending. However, some interest-rate-sensitive sectors like residential investment have declined, and the recent rise in mortgage rates appears to be dragging home construction and sales down further. Consumer spending has strengthened this year, despite softness in real incomes and declining sentiment, which are partly due to higher energy prices. Labor Market Conditions Labor market conditions look to have improved since last year. Over the course of this year, the unemployment rate has edged down to 4.1 percent in October, remaining close to my estimate of its natural rate. Job gains have been above last year's anemic pace, averaging about 80,000 per month through October, and have broadened across industries beyond health care and social assistance. The labor market continues to show low dynamism, with low-hiring and low-firing conditions as we sometimes see in a late-cycle expansion. The job-finding rate has been low, especially for new labor force entrants, and the share of long-term unemployed workers has moved up significantly. Workers' perceptions of job availability in the Conference Board survey have remained soft in recent months. On their own, these data would be consistent with a higher unemployment rate than currently reported. However, layoffs have moved down this year, offsetting the softness in hiring. In plain terms, workers are both less likely to find a new job and less likely to be laid off, a somewhat unusual pattern. Although stable, the labor market does not appear to be tight, as wage growth has slowed to a modest pace. On a 12-month basis, the wages and salaries component of the employment cost index increased 3.1 percent in September, the same pace as the change in average hourly earnings for October. Both measures have slowed noticeably from a year ago. An increasing number of workers have taken on a supplemental part-time job to make ends meet, as the share of multiple job holders has increased back to levels seen in early 2025. Given strong productivity gains in recent years, wage growth at this pace is in line with or even below the pace we would expect if inflation was running at 2 percent. Inflation Progress on lowering inflation has stalled over the past two years or so. Today's consumer price index suggests that 12-month core PCE inflation likely moved up further to 3.3 percent in October, as upward pressures from higher energy prices and AI-related demand continue to flow through to core goods and services prices. Lack of progress on lowering inflation largely reflects a confluence of shocks unrelated to conditions in the labor market. Tariffs, energy, and AI-related price pressures each accounted for roughly one-fourth of above-target core PCE inflation over the 12 months ending in September. The remaining one-fourth likely reflects persistent effects from the inflationary shocks in recent years. Price pressures had been concentrated in a few categories, but the latest data suggest that these pressures may be broadening. It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations. But today's consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer. Tariff effects should further wane going forward. Energy-related price pressures should unwind when the Middle East conflict resolves. And inflation pressures related to the AI buildout seem to persist despite some early signs of slowing. I mostly view these pressures as reflecting relative price shocks in specific sectors of the economy. For example, the AI buildout has quickly shifted investment demand toward specific types of high-tech capital, putting upward pressure on prices due to relatively inelastic supply in the near term. As these shocks wane or unwind and with no inflationary pressures emerging in the labor market, my forecast is for core PCE inflation to move closer to 2 percent next year. Financial Conditions Financial conditions have tightened a bit recently because of lower equity prices, higher private interest rates, and a stronger dollar. That tightening comes against a backdrop of increased market volatility. Corporate bond and mortgage rate spreads have widened, and equity valuations in the tech sector have dropped, as investors appear to be reassessing expected returns and the risks associated with increased external financing for AI investment projects. Economic Outlook and Risks Looking ahead, my expectation is that policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence. These policies include pragmatic regulations, lower taxes, and more supportive policies toward businesses. I expect the labor market to remain stable and inflation to slow, as special factors currently holding inflation elevated gradually wane or unwind next year. Over time, I also expect increased AI adoption to raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation as lower production costs are passed through to consumer prices. On risks to the outlook, with the labor market improving since last year, I am more attentive to the inflation side of our mandate. Sustained supply-chain pressures from the AI buildout or greater pass-through of higher energy costs could cause inflation pressures to persist. I can also envision a scenario in which the effects of the Middle East conflict and the tech investment boom wane or unwind quickly. In this scenario, I would also expect a timelier return of core PCE inflation toward our target. I also see a number of risks to the outlook for economic activity, many originating in financial markets. These risks include a large correction in equity valuations, if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations, and a sharp increase in private longer-term interest rates. Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending. And higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment. I will continue to closely monitor developments in credit and equity markets to assess risks to economic growth and financial stability. Important Issues for Monetary Policy I see conditions in energy markets and the AI buildout as two important issues for the economy in the months ahead. Developments in these two areas could have material effects on both sides of our mandate and could influence my views on the path for monetary policy. Energy Markets The Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets, impairing the flow of oil and other commodities passing through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for about 20 percent of global oil supply before the conflict—roughly equivalent to total U.S. oil consumption. As tensions rose, Brent oil prices moved up to and above $110 per barrel in the second half of October before dropping sharply last week on optimism that an agreement between the U.S. and Iran could be reached following the midterm elections. Although crude oil flows in the Persian Gulf have recovered to near pre-conflict levels in recent weeks, freight rates and insurance premiums have surged because of more complex logistics and ongoing geopolitical risk, raising the cost of delivered oil to many markets around the world. Prices for gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel also moved up to near or even above their highs in the spring. These higher prices reflected both higher crude oil prices and wider refining margins, as refineries in both the Persian Gulf and Russia have been damaged as a result of ongoing military conflicts in both regions. Prices for refined products have retraced some of the earlier gains more recently as crude oil prices have receded and margins have shown signs of normalizing. While the outcomes of these conflicts remain uncertain, my approach is to look through temporary energy-driven inflation, when possible, and to remain alert to signs that it is spreading into broader prices or expectations. If geopolitical tensions persist, energy prices may stay elevated in the near term, increasing risks that core inflation may also stay elevated because of increased pass-through to consumer prices of higher production and transportation costs. Although the U.S. economy is now a net exporter of oil products and less energy intensive, we could still see an impact on economic activity from higher energy prices. The recent deterioration in consumer sentiment measures suggests households may be internalizing a more persistent reduction in their purchasing power. I would be especially concerned about effects on both sides of our mandate if there were further significant disruptions to energy markets. An escalation of geopolitical tensions could have more meaningful effects on real activity because of higher uncertainty and the larger impact of energy prices on lower- and middle-income consumers. Even with a quick resolution to the Middle East conflict, it may take some time for energy prices to normalize. Futures markets expect oil prices to decline only gradually, as global oil consumption is projected to exceed supply at least through the end of this year. As inventories have been drawn down, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has reached a bit less than 50 days of crude oil imports, the lowest level since the early 1980s, reflecting both this year's and the larger 2022 SPR releases. A number of new Gulf pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz are under construction or expansion, with the United Arab Emirates' West–East expansion coming online in early 2027 and most others in 2028 and beyond. Domestic oil production could also continue to rise, which would put downward pressure on fuel costs. AI Buildout In remarks earlier this year, I discussed the responsible use of AI in the financial system. 4 Today I will describe how this technology is shaping the broader economy. Given the transformative promise of this technology, investment in data centers has boomed and has been a major influence on the U.S. economy. With plans for new data centers continuing to surge, I expect the AI shock to play out over some time. However, as these investments are increasingly being financed with external funds, including off-balance-sheet liabilities, I am also focused on potential risks to the economy and financial stability if revenues from AI customers disappoint. We may still be in the early days when investment rises rapidly while workers and firms determine the best use cases before we see more meaningful effects on productivity. The boom in data center investment is undeniable, with growth in real business fixed investment strengthening further this year to a pace like the 1990s tech boom. High-tech equipment, software, and data center construction have accounted for the large majority of growth in business investment since 2025, with gains broadening to other categories this year. AI adoption has grown significantly, especially among larger firms, with about 25 percent of businesses and roughly 10 percent of workers reporting using AI every day in their work. However, use varies greatly across industries and occupations, with stronger adoption in information and other business services sectors. I think there is a risk that some workers will be displaced as firms adopt this technology, even as others see their productivity—and wages—rise. Monetary policy cannot address that transition directly, but it should support a dynamic labor market that facilitates the necessary retraining and mobility of workers across jobs. AI revenues have been rising quickly but are not yet sufficient to pay for the expense of maintaining existing and developing new AI models and data centers. As capital spending has surged, hyperscalers and other companies have increasingly been sourcing funds from credit and equity markets. And as investors see an increased risk in these investments, the cost of financing has been rising notably. In addition to financing costs, the AI buildout is also putting upward pressure on a number of price categories. Prices of memory chips, semiconductors, computers, and other electronic products have increased sharply this year—in a few categories by double digits—as demand from data centers has outpaced supply. I expect production capacity to catch up to demand gradually over time. AI-related debt has been rising rapidly, with notable gains in corporate bonds, private credit, and project finance, and is on track to exceed $800 billion this year. Other obligations, in the form of long-term lease and contract commitments and residual value guarantees, have also surged and their potential payments are estimated at more than three times the amount of debt. Given their strong credit ratings, hyperscalers and large tech firms have assumed off-balance-sheet liabilities to allow smaller and riskier companies to use them as collateral in asset-based financing for data center construction and the purchase of accelerated computing equipment. These connections among AI firms have also been accompanied by hyperscalers and chip designers making equity investments in smaller companies that purchase their products, creating the appearance of circular financing. The largest U.S. bank holding companies have some exposure to AI-related financing, which is scrutinized during annual supervisory stress tests. Life insurance companies, pension funds, private credit, and mutual funds also have exposure. Most of these entities are well capitalized and have stable funding. But the complex nature of the financing structures makes it difficult to properly assess counterparty risk. Risks seem to be concentrated in only a few large firms that provide AI services, including AI labs and the hyperscalers. If AI-related revenues fall short of sharply rising costs, especially as public sentiment and local opposition could lead to increased regulation and delays, we could see a sharp correction in equity prices for AI firms, higher financing costs, and reduced access to credit. This shock would likely slow the AI buildout and soften both economic activity and inflation. We may have already seen some reassessment of expected returns play out in recent weeks as equity valuations dropped, corporate bond spreads widened, and credit default swaps increased for some companies involved in the AI buildout. I will be looking at how momentum in adoption of and investment in this technology evolves and for possible effects on both inflation and employment. The Path Forward for Monetary Policy As we think about the path ahead, it is important to remember that over the past two years the U.S. economy has experienced successive inflationary shocks that have not been driven by labor market conditions. Monetary policy cannot offset the direct effects of tariffs and energy costs on inflation, but it plays a central role in containing the second-round effects. Monetary policy also has limited influence on AI-related price pressures. However, in certain segments of AI-intensive sectors, particularly among newer and medium-sized firms, higher interest rates appear to be holding back investment and purchasing decisions. As I noted earlier, financial conditions have tightened. Against this backdrop, the benefit of additional policy tightening has to be carefully weighed against its costs for interest-rate-sensitive sectors. The October Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices (SLOOS) suggests that the concentration of demand weakness in real estate loan categories reflects existing headwinds in those sectors. 5 Time will help us learn more about the durability of momentum in AI-related demand and the evolution of geopolitical risks, both of which could be critical in the months ahead for setting our policy stance. Greater clarity on AI-related financing conditions and the sustainability of AI investments should increase my confidence in future policy decisions. Geopolitical conditions affect commodity markets and the degree of economic uncertainty perceived by households and businesses. Before our next meeting in December, we will receive the PCE inflation report for October and the employment report for November. Today, I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming. This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2 percent. Given the recent market volatility, I will also continue to closely monitor how developments in financial conditions influence the economic outlook. In the meantime, I will continue to meet with a broad range of contacts to inform my assessment of economic conditions and the appropriate stance of policy. It is important to remember that monetary policy is not on a preset course. At each FOMC meeting, my colleagues and I will evaluate incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the implications for the risks to our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and price stability. Thank you again for the invitation to join you this afternoon. I look forward to our discussion. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Note that currently reported GDP growth in the first half of this year may be overestimated by about 0.3 percentage point, reflecting downward revisions in the retail sales annual update that were not folded into the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) 2026 annual revision of the national accounts.
