title: Honduran National Unlawfully Residing in the United States Pleads Guilty to Fentanyl Trafficking and Firearm Charges
body: Press Release Honduran National Unlawfully Residing in the United States Pleads Guilty to Fentanyl Trafficking and Firearm Charges Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Oregon PORTLAND, Ore. — A Honduran national unlawfully residing in the United States pleaded guilty in federal court today to possessing fentanyl with the intent to distribute and unlawfully possessing a firearm, announced U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford. Ingrid Hernandez-Salgado , 22, of Gresham, Oregon, pleaded guilty to one count of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. “Fentanyl continues to devastate families and communities across Oregon, and those who choose to distribute this deadly drug will be held accountable,” said U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford. “This defendant not only trafficked fentanyl but also possessed a stolen firearm while unlawfully present in the United States. Federal, state, and local law enforcement partners remain committed to disrupting drug trafficking and protecting public safety.” According to court documents, in July 2026, an undercover Portland Police Bureau officer began communicating by text message with Hernandez-Salgado after investigators identified a phone number believed to be used in drug trafficking. Over several days, Hernandez-Salgado and the undercover officer negotiated the sale of approximately one ounce of fentanyl powder and agreed to meet on July 8, 2026, near a gas station in Gresham, Oregon. Law enforcement officers conducting surveillance observed Hernandez-Salgado arrive at the meeting location in a vehicle. After confirming she was the individual communicating with the undercover officer, officers detained her and recovered approximately 25 grams of fentanyl powder. During a search of the vehicle, investigators located a stolen AMT Backup .45 ACP pistol in the vehicle's center console. Following Hernandez-Salgado's arrest, investigators searched her apartment in Gresham and located more than $5,900 in U.S. currency. As part of her guilty plea, Hernandez-Salgado admitted that she knowingly possessed fentanyl with the intent to distribute it and knowingly possessed a firearm while unlawfully present in the United States. She further admitted that the firearm had traveled in interstate commerce and that she knew of her unlawful immigration status when she possessed it. Under the terms of the plea agreement, Hernandez-Salgado agreed to forfeit the firearm, associated ammunition, approximately $5,919 in U.S. currency, and two cellular phones during the investigation. Hernandez-Salgado faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison for possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and 15 years in federal prison for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. This case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the Portland Police Bureau. It is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Cassady Adams for the District of Oregon. ### Updated November 10, 2026 Topic Drug Trafficking Component USAO - Oregon

title: Portland Man Sentenced to 55 Months in Federal Prison for Mail Theft, Identity Theft Scheme
body: Press Release Portland Man Sentenced to 55 Months in Federal Prison for Mail Theft, Identity Theft Scheme Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Oregon PORTLAND, Ore. — A Portland man was sentenced to four years and seven months in federal prison for stealing hundreds of pieces of mail, using stolen identities to commit bank fraud, and possessing counterfeit postal service keys, U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford announced today. Michael John Peters , 43, was sentenced to 55 months in federal prison and three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to possession of stolen mail, possession of counterfeit postal service arrow keys, bank fraud, and aggravated identity theft. The court also ordered Peters to pay $30,079 in restitution to victims and a $400 special assessment. According to court documents, beginning in May 2025, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service investigated a series of mail thefts from apartment and condominium buildings throughout the Portland metropolitan area. Surveillance footage showed Peters entering secured residential buildings, opening cluster mailboxes using counterfeit postal service keys, and stealing mail. On July 8, 2025, Peters was confronted by security staff while attempting another mail theft. He abandoned a backpack containing counterfeit postal service keys, stolen mail belonging to multiple victims, and a device used to gain access to secured buildings. Investigators determined that Peters used information obtained from stolen mail to commit identity theft and bank fraud. In one instance, he opened a checking account in a victim's name and obtained a $20,000 loan from a financial institution. He also submitted additional fraudulent loan applications seeking more than $100,000 from various financial institutions. On Sept. 22, 2025, U.S. Postal Inspectors executed a federal search warrant at an apartment Peters had rented using a victim's identity. When authorities arrived, a tenant reported that Peters jumped from an upper-floor balcony onto the tenant's twelfth-floor balcony before running through the apartment and fleeing down a stairwell. During the search, investigators recovered approximately 393 pieces of stolen mail, 22 identification cards, 15 gift cards, 15 debit and credit cards, counterfeit identification documents, and equipment used to manufacture counterfeit keys and fraudulent identification cards. Authorities also seized 3D printers, a key-cutting machine, credit card readers, silicone key molds, and other tools used to facilitate the scheme. Investigators later arrested Peters at the residence of a romantic partner and recovered additional evidence of the identity theft operation from his cellular phones. Court records show Peters had prior convictions for similar offenses in Hawaii and California and was on probation in both jurisdictions when he committed the Oregon offenses. The case was investigated by the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, with assistance from the Portland Police Bureau and the U.S. Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA). It was prosecuted by First Assistant U.S. Attorney William M. Narus for the District of Oregon. Updated November 10, 2026 Component USAO - Oregon

title: Kalihi Man Sentenced to Over Nine Years in Prison for  Gunpoint Game Room Robbery
body: Press Release Kalihi Man Sentenced to Over Nine Years in Prison for  Gunpoint Game Room Robbery Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Hawaii HONOLULU – United States Attorney Ken Sorenson announced that Chris Pham, 22, of Kalihi, Oahu, was sentenced on November 9, 2026, by Senior United States District Judge Helen Gillmor to 111 months in federal prison for Hobbs Act robbery and brandishing a firearm during the commission of the robbery, followed by five years of supervised release. As admitted in the plea agreement, on or about December 27, 2024, the defendant robbed approximately $3,000 from an illegal game room in Honolulu, brandishing a firearm at the operators and patrons of the game room and threatening to shoot if they moved.  He later admitted to displaying a loaded privately made firearm, or “ghost gun,” during the course of the robbery.  He was arrested in March 2025 in possession of a separate firearm and ammunition. “Illegal game rooms are a hotbed of violence and criminal activity, attracting people like Chris Pham who see them as cash-rich targets for armed robbery,” said U.S. Attorney Ken Sorenson.  “In coordination with our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners, we will continue to dismantle and disrupt illegal game rooms on the islands and prosecute any criminal activity we find associated with them.” “This sentence reflects the serious threat posed by violent offenders who choose to arm themselves while engaging in criminal activity,” said FBI Honolulu Special Agent in Charge Tom Ryan.  “The defendant’s actions related to robbery and illegal firearm possession demonstrated a clear disregard for the safety of our community.  The FBI and our law enforcement partners remain committed to removing dangerous individuals and illegal weapons from our streets and holding offenders accountable for their actions.” The FBI investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael F. Albanese prosecuted the case. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe.  Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges.  As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe.  PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies.  These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Contact Aislinn Affinito Aislinn.Affinito@usdoj.gov Updated November 10, 2026 Topics Project Safe Neighborhoods Violent Crime Component USAO - Hawaii

title: Umatilla Man Sentenced to Seven Years in Federal Prison for Distributing Child Sexual Abuse Material and Making Hoax Abuse Reports
body: Press Release Umatilla Man Sentenced to Seven Years in Federal Prison for Distributing Child Sexual Abuse Material and Making Hoax Abuse Reports Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Oregon PORTLAND, Ore. — Thomas Goatley , 23, of Umatilla, was sentenced to 87 months in federal prison and five years of supervised release for distributing child sexual abuse material and making harassing phone calls in which he falsely claimed to be sexually abusing children, U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford announced today. According to court documents, from at least September 2023 through April 2024, Goatley used multiple online platforms, including Instagram, Facebook, Discord and X, to view, receive and distribute child sexual abuse material. When he was arrested in July 2024, investigators found approximately 50 images and 40 videos depicting the sexual abuse of children in his possession. Court records show Goatley also made numerous anonymous harassing phone calls to schools, police departments, emergency dispatch centers, animal shelters and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC). During the calls, he falsely claimed to be sexually abusing a child and provided fabricated details about the alleged abuse. Among other incidents, Goatley repeatedly contacted an elementary school in Helena, Montana, and falsely claimed to be abusing a student. He also called an elementary school in Newcastle, Wyoming, and falsely reported that he had abducted and was abusing a student. In response, schools in Newcastle were placed on lockdown while law enforcement officers from multiple agencies worked to locate the caller. Goatley also contacted the Dearborn, Michigan, Police Department and falsely claimed to be abusing his 12-year-old daughter at a local hotel. Officers responded and determined the room he described did not exist. Between Feb. 17 and April 8, 2024, Goatley made 10 calls to NCMEC falsely claiming to be abusing either his daughter or sister. During many of the calls, he provided false identifying information. On Aug. 12, 2026, Goatley waived indictment and pleaded guilty to a five-count information charging one count of distributing child pornography and four counts of making obscene or harassing telephone calls. In addition to the prison sentence, the court ordered Goatley to pay $1,000 to NCMEC, pay a $500 special assessment and forfeit digital devices used in the offenses. “Individuals who distribute child sexual abuse material contribute to the ongoing exploitation of children, while false reports of child abuse divert critical law enforcement resources and create fear in communities,” said U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford. “This sentence holds the defendant accountable for both harms.” The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. It was prosecuted by Mira Chernick, Assistant U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon. ### Updated November 10, 2026 Component USAO - Oregon

title: Colombian-Based Cocaine Importers Indicted in Drug Conspiracy and Conspiracy to Provide Material Support to the FARC
body: Press Release Colombian-Based Cocaine Importers Indicted in Drug Conspiracy and Conspiracy to Provide Material Support to the FARC Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Louisiana shane.jones@usdoj.gov New case brought as part of Homeland Security Task Force Operation Sail Away NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA – A third superseding indictment recently unsealed in the Eastern District of Louisiana charges six members and associates of a Colombian-Russian drug trafficking organization with federal drug trafficking offenses, including conspiring to import hundreds of kilograms of cocaine into the United States, announced U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle. The superseding indictment charges Russian nationals with conspiring to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization by means of their conspiracy to import hundreds of kilograms of cocaine into the United States from the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia, also known as the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia – People’s Army (FARC-EP). “Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) operations are, at their core, about one thing …protecting our communities from the very real threat of violence posed by drug trafficking organizations,” said U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle. “The shared mission of HSTF remains constant; to enforce the laws of the land and to protect the public that we are proud to serve.” The superseding indictment charges ALEXANDER ALTERGOTT, age 57, of Russia, LUCA DETTO, age 45, of Italy, OLEG KHAZOV , age 39, of Russia, DIAGO GOMEZ-MORILLO a/k/a EFATA , of Colombia, VITALII ZHIKHAREV , age 41, of Russia, and BORIS YAKOVLEV , of Russia, for violations of the Federal Controlled Substances Act, the Transnational Drug Trafficking Act. Additionally, it charges these individuals with Conspiracy to Provide Material Support to a Foreign Terrorist Organization. The third superseding indictment added charges against ALTERGOTT’s co-conspirators. Count 1 charges ALTERGOTT, DETTO, KHAZOV , GOMEZ-MORILLO a/k/a EFATA , ZHIKHAREV , and YAKOVLEV with conspiring to distribute, and possess with intent to distribute, five kilograms or more of cocaine, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 841(a)(1), 841(b)(1)(A), and 846. Count 2 charges ALTERGOTT, DETTO, KHAZOV, and ZHIKHAREV with conspiring to distribute cocaine for the purpose of unlawfully importing it into the United States, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 959(a), 959(d), 960(a)(3), 960(b)(1)(B)(ii), and 963. Count 3 charges DETTO , KHAZOV, and ZHIKHAREV with distribution of cocaine for the purpose of unlawfully importing it into the United States, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 959(a), 959(d), 960(a)(3), and 960(b)(1)(B)(ii). Count 4 charges ALTERGOTT and ZHIKHAREV with conspiring to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia – People’s Army (FARC-EP). FARC-EP is a dissident faction of the FARC terrorist group and emerged after its rejection of a 2016 peace agreement between FARC and the Colombian government. FARC-EP is Colombia’s most powerful and violent dissident group and has continued to carry out criminal acts, including assassinations, extortion, hostage-takings, and armed assaults. The group focuses most of its attacks on Colombian government and military targets but has also attacked critical infrastructure, Colombian civilians, and U.S. military personnel in the country. FARC-EP equips its members with firearms, machine guns, mines, and bombs. The United States designated FARC-EP a foreign terrorist organization in December 2021. FARC-EP partners with other terrorist organizations, including the Sinaloa Cartel, Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG), and Nueva Familia Michoacana. For Count 1, ALTERGOTT, DETTO , KHAZOV, ZHIKHAREV, YAKOVLEV , and GOMEZ-MORILLO each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years, up to life imprisonment, a fine of up to $10,000,000, and at least 5 years of supervised release. For Count 2, ALTERGOTT, DETTO, KHAZOV , and ZHIKHAREV each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years, up to life imprisonment, a fine of up to $10,000,000, and at least 5 years of supervised release. For Count 3, DETTO , KHAZOV, and ZHIKHAREV each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years, up to life imprisonment, a fine of up to $10,000,000, and at least 5 years of supervised release. For Count 4, ALTERGOTT and ZHIKHAREV each face up to 20 years in prison, up to a $250,000 fine, and up to 3 years of supervised release. Each of these individuals also faces payment of a $100 mandatory special assessment fee per charged count. United States Attorney David I. Courcelle reiterated that the third superseding indictment is merely an allegation and that the guilt of the defendants must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. This case is being investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration and additional assistance was provided by the Justice Department’s Judicial Attaché Office in Bogotá and Office of International Affairs who worked with the Cuerpo Técnico de Investigación of the Colombian Attorney General’s Office. Assistant United States Attorney Rachal Cassagne of the Narcotics Unit is in charge of the prosecution. Participating Agencies: Domestic Investigative Agencies: Drug Enforcement Administration Federal Bureau of Investigation Homeland Security Investigation United States Border Patrol United States Marshals Service Louisiana State Police Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office Gretna Police Department Kenner Police Department International Investigative Agencies: DEA Offices in Cartagena, Colombia; and Rome, Italy. The Colombian National Police Italian National Police. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF New Orleans comprises agents and officers from the Department of Homeland Security, Federal Bureau of Investigations, Drug Enforcement Administration and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana. *      *      * Contact Shane M. title: Trucking company owner charged in labor scheme involving unauthorized non-citizen drivers
body: Press Release Trucking company owner charged in labor scheme involving unauthorized non-citizen drivers Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Texas LAREDO, Texas – A 56-year-old Laredo man has been indicted for allegedly employing unauthorized drivers to transport domestic freight. Armando Martinez Varela faces charges involving employment of unauthorized workers, encouraging or inducing unlawful entry or residence, harboring aliens, and making materially false statements to federal investigators. According to the indictment, Varela owned VMS Transport LLC and recruited drivers admitted under B-1 nonimmigrant status to transport domestic freight without authorization. The drivers allegedly picked up trailers in Laredo and delivered shipments throughout the United States. B-1 status permits certain temporary business activities, including qualifying international transportation, but does not authorize employment transporting freight solely within the United States. The indictment further alleges Varela arranged housing for drivers between assignments rather than having them return to Mexico. Between Feb. 20 and May 15, VMS records allegedly showed 1,044 domestic transportation trips involving 57 B-1 visa drivers. The charges allege VMS paid these drivers 25 to 50 cents per mile, compared with 70 cents for authorized drivers performing similar work. The arrangement saved the company approximately $299,606 in labor costs, according to the allegations. If convicted, Varela faces up to 10 years in federal prison and a possible $250,000 maximum fine. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Christine A. Cortez is prosecuting the case. An indictment is a formal accusation of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless convicted through due process of law. Updated November 10, 2026 Component USAO - Texas, Southern

title: Anchorage Woman Sentenced to 5 Years in Prison for Wire Fraud  and Aggravated Identity Theft
body: Press Release Anchorage Woman Sentenced to 5 Years in Prison for Wire Fraud  and Aggravated Identity Theft Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Alaska ANCHORAGE, Alaska – An Anchorage woman was sentenced today to 5 years in prison for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft followed by 5 years of supervised release.  Payment of restitution to the victims in the case was also ordered. According to court documents, between February 2021 and February 2022, Dusty Starr, 48, carried out a scheme to defraud victims and obtain money using stolen identifications. The defendant’s scheme involved mail theft, identity theft, creation of fraudulent email and financial accounts, production of forged checks, and the submission of false applications to obtain COVID rental relief funds. The defendant possessed more than 170 identities stolen from the mail, from vehicles, and from individuals to carry out her fraud.  Using these stolen identities Starr created email accounts, bank accounts, money‑transfer accounts, and sham business entities to impersonate victims and route proceeds from her fraud into accounts under her control. The total estimated loss from the defendant’s fraud is more than $71,000, A significant portion of the defendant’s scheme centered on exploiting an Alaska state agency that provides rental assistance and helped distribute rent relief in coordination with charitable organizations during the pandemic.  The defendant fraudulently posed as multiple different landlords and tenants, using stolen identities to submit nine fraudulent applications. The state agency disbursed $47,550 in payments to accounts that Starr opened using stolen identities. Also, as part of her fraud scheme, Starr used stolen mail and stolen identities to forge and negotiate fraudulent checks on the accounts of several Alaska Native corporations. Starr created forged checks using authentic account information obtained from legitimate checks stolen from the mail together with check-printing equipment she purchased from Amazon, then she deposited the forged checks into accounts opened using stolen identities. Losses to these organizations total more than $24,000. “The defendant carried out a scheme using stolen identities to fraudulently obtain pandemic relief and to steal money from several Alaska Native corporations, among others. Our office will continue to prioritize pursuing abuses of pandemic relief and to protect the sanctity of the U.S. Postal Service critical to so many Alaskans” said Michael J. Heyman, U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska. “The U.S. Postal Inspection Service remains committed to ensuring the security and integrity of the mail system. The sentencing of Starr leaves a clear and lasting message for the fraudsters of Alaska that they have no place in the U.S. Postal Service and the State of Alaska," said Jarrod Resendez, Acting Inspector in Charge of the Seattle Division of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. "The U.S. Postal Inspection Service will not sit back while individuals like Starr exploit the postal system to harm our communities, we will hold them accountable. We thank our partners in law enforcement for their support and efforts in this investigation.” “Theft can be financially devastating for victims, and the effects can last long after the crime. Anchorage Police Department fraud detective, Tiffani Loughman, spent years pursuing this case because the people and organizations harmed deserved answers and accountability. We’re grateful to our federal partners for helping see it through to sentencing," said Chief Sean Case, Anchorage Police Department. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service and the Anchorage Police Department investigated the case with assistance from the U.S. Postal Service, Office of Inspector General. Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrea Steward prosecuted the case. ### Contact Contact: USAAK-Press Release Public Affairs Office usaak.pressrelease@usdoj.gov Updated November 10, 2026 Component USAO - Alaska

title: U.S. Attorneys Create Task Force to Combat Fraud
body: Press Release U.S. Attorneys Create Task Force to Combat Fraud Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of West Virginia CLARKSBURG, WEST VIRGINIA – U.S. Attorneys Matthew L. Harvey and Moore Capito have joined with other federal, state, and local partners to create the Mountain State Fraud and Diversion Task Force, which will tirelessly combat fraud across the state of West Virginia. Fraud costs consumers billions of dollars each year, raising the costs of insurance premiums, healthcare costs, and the costs of other goods, as well as depleting the retirement funds and savings of victims across the country. “Fraud comes with too high a cost for the average American, and West Virginians work too hard to lose money to fraudsters,” said U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey. “This task force will collaborate to fight fraud in every corner - from healthcare to insurance to tax to personal fraud. If you are scheming, we will find you, charge you, and convict you.” “My first year as U.S. Attorney made it clear to me how serious a threat fraud poses to West Virginians and how fighting it requires all of us to work together across the state,” said U.S. Attorney Moore Capito. “That’s why we joined together with the Northern District to form the Mountain State Fraud and Diversion Task Force. Ahead of today’s inaugural meeting, we held a series of roundtables with local prosecutors and law enforcement officers across our district. Our on-the-ground partners gave us an invaluable perspective on the ways fraud is affecting their communities and helped us understand where and how this task force can be most effective. By working together across district lines, we’ll be better positioned to uncover fraud, protect taxpayers, and make sure those who commit fraud answer for it.” The Mountain State Fraud Task Force comprises both U.S. Attorney’s Offices in West Virginia, federal, state, and local law enforcement, and the West Virginia Attorney General’s Office. U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey and U.S. Attorney Moore Capito, along with Assistant U.S. Attorneys from each office, offered insight to the work done to combat fraud every day, sharing successes and monies recovered. At the meeting, the National Fraud Detection Center spoke of trends, investigative techniques and abilities, and resources available to all law enforcement. The National Fraud Enforcement Division also shared information about its mission, partnerships, analytics, and asset recovery resources. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the formation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division, which focuses on investigating and prosecuting fraud against the American public. This effort supports the President’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole‑of‑government initiative chaired by the Vice President to address fraud, waste, and abuse in federal benefit programs. The inaugural Mountain State Fraud and Diversion Task Force meeting was held at the FBI Criminal Justice Information Services facility in Clarksburg, West Virginia. The task force plans to meet bi-annually. Updated November 10, 2026 Topics Community Outreach Fraud Components USAO - West Virginia, Northern USAO - West Virginia, Southern

title: Former Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation Employee Sentenced for Housing Assistance Fraud Scheme
body: Press Release Former Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation Employee Sentenced for Housing Assistance Fraud Scheme Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Pennsylvania PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Latonia Reed, 41, of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was sentenced today to two years of probation, community service, and restitution of $14,400 by United States District Judge Joel H. Slomsky for a scheme to defraud the City of Philadelphia and the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation (“PHDC”), Reed’s then-employer. The defendant was charged by information with one count of wire fraud and pleaded guilty in June of this year. As detailed in court filings and statements, beginning in 2021, Reed worked as a financial specialist and program analyst at the PHDC, a community development organization that offered housing assistance to Philadelphians, including rental assistance, grants to first-time home buyers, investments in neighborhood preservation projects, loans to landlords to make improvements to affordable housing units, free home adaptations for low-income city residents with physical disabilities, and funding for affordable housing development projects. Between July 10, 2024, and February 2025, while she worked at the PHDC, the defendant carried out a scheme to defraud the organization and the city for the benefit of Person 1, by drafting, submitting, and approving four false housing assistance applications, which resulted in payments to Person 1 totaling approximately $14,400. Reed completed each of the applications with false information, including the names and phone numbers of fake tenants, and created bogus supporting documents, such as a rent ledger which purported to show the dates and amounts of rent payments and arrears for tenants she knew to be fake. Reed also forged the signatures of the fake tenants on agreements, affidavits, and notices submitted with the four fraudulent assistance applications. This case was investigated by the FBI and the Philadelphia Office of the Inspector General and prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Nancy E. Potts. body: Waze Waze and Garmin team up to boost driver awareness of cyclists. Nov 10, 2026 Waze and Garmin are launching real-time cycling alerts to help create a safer environment on the road. Now, when cyclists turn on Garmin LiveTrack™ on their Garmin Edge® bike computer or Garmin smartwatch, they can choose to show up as a real-time, moving icon on Waze for extra peace of mind. Drivers will also see a notification when a cyclist is nearby, giving them a helpful reminder to slow down, stay aware, and share the road thoughtfully. This feature is completely opt-in and built with privacy in mind. Drivers only see a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby — never information about a specific cyclist or route. title: Previously Convicted Mexican National Unlawfully Residing in the United States Sentenced to Five Years in Federal Prison for Distributing Methamphetamine in Oregon
body: Press Release Previously Convicted Mexican National Unlawfully Residing in the United States Sentenced to Five Years in Federal Prison for Distributing Methamphetamine in Oregon Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Oregon PORTLAND, Ore. — Fernando Lombera Gonzalez , 34, a Mexican national unlawfully residing in the United States, was sentenced to 63 months in federal prison and five years of supervised release today for conspiring to distribute more than three pounds of methamphetamine in Oregon. According to court documents, in late May 2024, a federal agent contacted Gonzalez and arranged a controlled purchase of approximately 1,350 grams of methamphetamine. On June 1, 2024, Gonzalez traveled to Salem, Oregon, where Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) investigators observed him retrieve methamphetamine from a second vehicle before delivering approximately 1,377 grams of the drug, roughly equivalent to three pounds, in exchange for payment. A federal arrest warrant was issued for Gonzalez in November 2024. On Jan. 18, 2025, Gonzalez was encountered during a traffic stop and provided law enforcement officers with a false name. Despite the deception, officers identified Gonzalez and arrested him on an outstanding warrant in a separate Marion County case involving a convicted felon in possession of a firearm. He was later transferred to federal custody in this case. On Nov. 13, 2025, Gonzalez pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance. Court records show Gonzalez had previously been convicted of methamphetamine trafficking and removed from the United States to Mexico. After unlawfully returning to the United States, he resumed criminal activity and served as a middleman for a large-scale drug trafficking organization operating in the Salem area. Prosecutors noted that neither his prior felony drug trafficking conviction nor his removal from the United States deterred him from returning to drug trafficking. Prosecutors further noted that Gonzalez engaged in separate firearm-related criminal conduct as a convicted felon, including an incident in which he discharged a firearm outside a nightclub. “After a felony drug trafficking conviction and removal from the United States, this defendant unlawfully returned and went right back to serious criminal conduct,” said U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford. “Not only did he distribute large quantities of methamphetamine – a drug that fuels addiction, violence, and suffering in our communities – but he also engaged in separate firearm-related criminal activity as a convicted felon. Repeat offenders who show this level of disregard for our laws and public safety will be prosecuted aggressively and held accountable." This case was investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Julia Jarrett of the District of Oregon. Updated November 10, 2026 Topic Drug Trafficking Component USAO - Oregon

title: Porter woman sentenced for fraud, threats, and assault of an officer after fraudulently receiving $435,000 new home
body: Press Release Porter woman sentenced for fraud, threats, and assault of an officer after fraudulently receiving $435,000 new home Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Texas DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division investigates and prosecutes those who commit fraud against the American people. HOUSTON – A 56-year-old local resident has been ordered to federal prison for wire fraud, fraud in connection with a major disaster, threatening to kill a witness, and assaulting/impeding a law enforcement officer. Sharai Poteet pleaded guilty June 1. U.S. District Judge Kenneth Hoyt ordered Poteet to serve 71 months in federal prison to be immediately followed by three years of supervised release. She must also pay $537,209 in restitution to the Department of Housing and Urban Development and Federal Emergency Management Agency. At the hearing, the court considered additional evidence and testimony that described the devasting emotional impact her threats have had on the victim and victim’s family as well as forgeries she committed after being charged with these crimes. The evidence also demonstrated Poteet’s brazen disregard for the law, including an internet search she conducted asking “what is the punishment for lying to FEMA,” followed shortly after by her submission of a fraudulent application to FEMA for hurricane disaster relief. In handing down the sentence, the court noted the lengthy duration of her crimes as well as the “complete disregard” for who her actions hurt, including placing her family members at risk of prosecution. The court commented that “without being charged, it is unlikely she would have stopped” her despicable behavior. “Sharai Poteet exploited programs intended to assist vulnerable hurricane victims and used those funds for her own personal enrichment,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz. “When individuals steal taxpayer-funded resources meant to help those in need, they are not just committing fraud—they are undermining the systems that keep families safe and communities stable.” “Sharai Poteet exploited HUD’s disaster recovery programs intended to help Hurricane Harvey victims and then attempted to obstruct accountability for her crimes,” said Deputy Assistant Inspector General for Investigations Robert Lawler with HUD, Office of Inspector General. “Rather than accept responsibility, Poteet used violence and intimidation against a whistleblower and a federal agent carrying out lawful duties. HUD-OIG will continue to work with the U.S. Attorney’s Office and our law enforcement partners to vigorously pursue those who seek to profit by abusing HUD-funded programs.” “Under President Trump, fraudsters are facing the consequences for stealing from taxpayers,” said Deputy Secretary Andrew Hughes of U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. “Despite her attempts to evade the law, Sharai Poteet is finally being held accountable for abusing HUD disaster relief funds, lying to obtain a newly built home valued at nearly half a million dollars, and stealing from those who lost everything in Hurricane Harvey. Fraudsters beware: HUD will leave no stone unturned until every dollar is accounted for and justice is served.” From 2019 through 2024, Poteet engaged in a scheme to fraudulently obtain disaster-relief housing assistance and additional federal benefits. During the investigation, she also threatened to kill a witness and assaulted a federal officer. Poteet submitted fraudulent loan applications claiming 11 people—including seven children and a disabled adult—were members of her household. As a result of the false claims, Poteet received assistance in the form of a custom seven-bedroom home. The funds used to construct the home were intended to help Hurricane Harvey victims through a HUD program. The home Poteet received was the largest the program had built at that time. The investigation revealed Poteet also submitted five fraudulent applications for disaster assistance from the FEMA for storms that occurred between 2017 and 2024. During the investigation, she threatened a whistleblower in an attempt to silence them. Poteet also assaulted a federal agent while attempting to flee during an operation intended to seize her cell phone. Poteet was ordered into custody following the sentencing. HUD-OIG conducted the investigation. Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Shalimar Addy prosecuted the case. The Department of Justice has created the National Fraud Enforcement Division . The core mission of the Fraud Division is to zealously investigate and prosecute those who steal or fraudulently misuse taxpayer dollars. Department of Justice efforts to combat fraud support President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste and abuse within federal benefit programs. Updated November 10, 2026 Topic Disaster Fraud Components National Fraud Enforcement Division USAO - Texas, Southern

title: Cheektowaga man arrested, charged with production of child pornography
body: Press Release Cheektowaga man arrested, charged with production of child pornography Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of New York BUFFALO, N.Y. – U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Bryce Weston, 22, of Cheektowaga, NY, was arrested and charged by criminal complaint with production of child sexual abuse material, which carries a minimum penalty of 15 years in prison, a maximum of 30 years, and a fine of $250,000. According to the criminal complaint, on August 23, 2026, Snapchat reported to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) that a file containing suspected child pornography was uploaded to its server. NCMEC generated a Cybertipline Report, which led to an investigation by the New York State Police Internet Crimes Against Children (NYSP ICAC) unit. The investigation subsequently traced the file to Bryce Weston. On October 14, 2026, the NYSP executed a search warrant at Weston’s Columbus Avenue residence. During an initial review of Weston’s cell phone, investigators recovered a chat conversation between Weston and a female individual who identified herself as a “minor” and a 13-year-old girl. Law enforcement found additional information related to Weston’s communications with the minor victim. During one of these communications, Weston identified himself as “Jake” and claimed he is “15 gonna be 16,” with the communication quickly turning sexual in nature. Weston subsequently sent a naked image of himself to the minor victim via text message. Weston also mentioned wanting to have sex with the minor victim. Weston continued to communicate with the minor victim, indicating that he wanted to meet with the minor victim in person. Weston stated during a conversation that he was 20 years old, with the minor victim again stating that she was 13 years old. Weston responded that he thought the minor victim was kidding about her age. Weston and the minor victim continued to communicate until October 2026. The communications were sexually explicit and included the exchange of multiple naked photos between Weston and the minor victim. Weston made an initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Jeremiah J. McCarthy and was held pending a detention hearing on November 12, 2026. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Andrew J. Scampoli and Franz M. Wright. The complaint is the result of an investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Allen D. Davis, II and the New York State Police, under the direction of Major Amie Feroleto. Additional assistance was provided by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty. # # # # Contact Barbara Burns 716-843-5817 Updated November 10, 2026 Topic Project Safe Neighborhoods Component USAO - New York, Western

title: Waller, The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism
body:

Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 10, 2026 The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism Governor Christopher J. Waller At the Bank of England Watchers Conference  King’s Business School and Money, Macro and Finance Society, London, United Kingdom Share Watch Live Thank you, Paul, and welcome to Bank of England watchers, who I suspect are watching the Federal Reserve as well. 1 My subject today is the outlook for the U.S. economy and the implications for monetary policy. I think there is little disagreement about the basics of that outlook. The U.S. economy is growing strongly, with a labor market that has brought employment close to its long-term rate. But inflation remains too high, so I will explain why I believe further tightening of monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2 percent in the medium term. The outline of my speech is to first explain why I voted to hold the policy rate steady at the most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Then I will talk about the general state of the U.S. economy. After that, I will ask some open-ended questions about the dynamism of the U.S. labor market that are important to consider over the longer run. I'll follow that by a discussion of recent inflation data and then describe my views about the future path of monetary policy. At our most recent meeting, I supported the FOMC majority in holding monetary policy at its current setting. As I said in a speech a couple weeks before then, my rationale was that the Committee's communication about the likely tightening of policy had already led financial markets to price in some tightening. 2 When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out—it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings. If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way. So, while the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does. Let me turn to the economy. Economic output continues to grow at a healthy pace. The initial estimate was that real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 3.4 percent in the third quarter, supported by strong consumer spending and robust investment. Consumption growth was helped by a booming stock market, and investment by businesses continued to surge, especially in high-tech equipment associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout. I expect GDP growth is backing off a bit in the current quarter, as consumer spending slows to levels that I think are more consistent with household income and wealth, but output will continue to grow at a solid pace. The labor market has also been solid. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent in October, the same rate it was over the summer. Job creation, which has been fluctuating widely month to month for some time, saw October gains of 165,000 jobs and 85,000 jobs added to estimates of the previous two months. To look through the volatility, the 6-month and 12-month average payroll gains have been closer to 80,000 jobs a month. This level is a bit above most estimates of the breakeven level needed to keep the unemployment rate steady but entirely consistent with my view that the supply and demand for labor are in rough balance. While the labor market has been stable, for over a year now it has been what is best characterized as "low hire, low fire." One can understand this characterization by looking at job separation and hiring rates today and comparing them with what they were before the pandemic (see figures 1 and 2 ). You will see that the rate of separations, the sum of layoffs and quits, has been persistently low the past few years compared with a decade ago. The hiring rate is also low. This is unusual because, in a strong labor market, the hiring rate is usually high. Hiring tends to be low when the labor market is weak, which is when the firing rate is often elevated. What is unusual today, and may be unprecedented, is the extent to which both firing and hiring are now so low. These data have led me to consider a question that has longer-term implications for the economy and monetary policy: Does a stable labor market necessarily mean it's a healthy labor market? To illustrate the difference, if your mom was in the hospital and the doctor told you her condition was stable, you would be relieved but you wouldn't say she is healthy. I am concerned that the low hire, low fire equilibrium in the labor market means it has lost some of its dynamism, which is important for productivity growth and real wages. If the labor market is in fact showing less dynamism, is it an issue for monetary policy? While I don't have answers to these questions, I do think the questions are worth asking. This discussion starts with distinguishing between net employment growth and gross flows in and out of employment. Behind the monthly job creation numbers that get most of the world's attention is the enormous churn in the labor market. For example, the 60,000 jobs created in September was a net change in the level of employment, but it is dwarfed by the more than 5 million people who left their jobs that month and the more than 5 million who were hired. Despite the low separation and hiring rates, the level of separations and hiring is huge. When I was a professor, I would use the following analogy for my students. If you stand by a river, you can measure the water level. If you return the next day and measure again, you will likely find that the water level is unchanged—it is stable. But in fact, a massive amount of water has flowed downstream since the day before. The same goes for the labor market—there is a lot of churning even if the level of employment is stable. The question is, does churn in the labor market matter? If so, is labor market churn bad or good? One could argue that this churn is inefficient. Why are people and firms wasting time swapping workers across jobs? If workers simply stayed at their firms, and firms never let them go, employment would be stable and resources would be saved from putting workers into new jobs. But would it mean the labor market is healthy? The answer is that the churn in hiring and firing is actually good for the economy. This churn reflects a dynamic market that allows labor resources to be allocated to more productive uses. If a worker and firm are not in a good, productive match, then it is more efficient and better for the economy for the worker and firm to separate and look for new partners. When more productive matches are formed, productivity, real wages, and profits will be higher. In this situation, employment may not be stable, but it is healthier. I believe this churn is what leads to the exceptional performance of the U.S. economy. The relative ease of starting businesses in the United States, compared with many other advanced economies, is a big advantage. The relative ease of firing employees, compared with many European Union economies, is surely not welcome by the workers affected, but cumulatively it was a factor that drove the stronger recovery in the United States from the pandemic recession. This flexibility in hiring and firing promotes a better match between skills of the worker and those demanded by businesses, making the most productive use of their abilities. As a result, this churn boosts the capacity of the economy and allows incomes to grow without inflationary pressure. So, given this discussion, how do we interpret the current low hire, low fire economy? Does it indicate that the U.S. labor market has become less dynamic and less healthy, which has implications for the economic outlook and for monetary policy? I will first consider the possible causes of this lower dynamism and then the possible implications. One explanation for the lower dynamism is that some of the decline in both hiring and firing may reflect, in part, a continuation of longer-run trends that were in place even before the pandemic. First, it is well known that the workforce is aging for a number of reasons: People are living longer and are healthier and more active at older ages; many members of the large post–World War II baby boom are in their 60s and 70s; and birth rates have declined, which increases the relative age of the workforce. This aging affects the dynamism of the labor market because older workers switch jobs less frequently, since many have managed over time to find better job matches and because older workers are less likely to relocate for work. The second trend is that the level of education of the workforce is increasing over time. More educated workers experience less job churn in general and, during downturns, face lower rates of job separations. Since 2010, the share of adults 25 and older with at least a bachelor's degree has increased from 28 percent to 37 percent. 3 If these were the only reasons for the decline in labor market dynamism, then it would be at a level consistent with these trend factors, suggesting an appropriate degree of dynamism with no implications for monetary policy. But the data suggest that, even after accounting for these factors, labor market dynamism still seems somewhat low. There are several possible reasons. One is that hiring and job-switching may have been restrained by the confluence of factors that have raised economic uncertainty since early 2025: the advent of AI, tariffs, changes in immigration policy and enforcement, and a general level of uncertainty about the economic outlook that has made business planning particularly challenging. One piece of evidence was a special question posed in the Federal Reserve's November 2025 Beige Book survey of economic conditions: Employers reported in November 2025 that hiring was unusually restrained because of uncertainty. I don't think uncertainty has diminished much since then. And another piece of evidence is in the most recent Beige Book, showing that several Fed Districts reported firms had delayed hiring or anticipate less job creation after investing in AI. Another reason for low dynamism is that low firing may be a consequence of the huge surge in job-switching from 2020 to 2023 related to the pandemic. Workers in new jobs are less inclined to change jobs again, and that may be limiting job-switching. If this is a large factor, it may be temporary—workers are in their jobs for a median of three years before switching again, and we are nearing that threshold for the last of the pandemic job switchers. But it's possible they could be staying longer now if the job-switching triggered by the pandemic had been unusually effective at improving the matches between workers and jobs—many relocated or chased dreams and new careers and may not be as willing to switch again. As you can tell, it is hard to pin down and properly weigh the possible causes of lower labor market dynamism and then judge how long that phenomenon might continue. This makes it hard to know the implications for the economic outlook and monetary policy. But we can talk more constructively, I think, about the possible effects of the current low hire, low fire environment. While low layoffs imply that fewer workers experience unemployment, a low hiring rate means that those who do become unemployed may experience longer unemployment spells. And, in fact, the percentage of unemployed people who have been looking for work for more than six months has climbed steadily since 2022 and is now quite elevated for a period of economic expansion. 4 Another logical consequence of lower dynamism in the labor market would be that new entrants, typically young and with less experience, are having a harder time finding jobs. I think anyone paying attention to the U.S. economy has been hearing about the challenges young workers are facing. Indeed, the share of new labor force entrants in unemployment has been rising and has reached close to the highest levels of the past twenty years. Both these developments may reflect a labor market that is not as healthy as the headline unemployment rate indicates, with implications for the longer-term path of monetary policy. If hires and separations are low because worker matches have improved, then this may be a boost to productivity and can be largely ignored in assessing the state of the labor market. But I worry that today's labor market dynamism may be low due to impediments to mobility that are affecting long-term and youth unemployment, and this may lead to a less-efficient distribution of workers across jobs, hindering productivity growth. This possibility is important to monitor because productivity growth is a crucial factor in judging how fast the economy can grow without undesirable inflationary pressure. As I said earlier, I don't have the answers to the questions I have posed, but I believe the questions are worth asking and addressing with more research. Let me put aside this discussion about the health of the labor market for now. What is important in the near term is that I see the labor market as stable and employment at a level close to the FOMC's maximum-employment goal. By contrast, inflation is well above 2 percent and the focus of my attention. For reasons I explained at the start of this speech, I was willing to wait to tighten monetary policy at the FOMC's October meeting. Inconveniently for today's event, we will get consumer price index (CPI) inflation for October in a few hours. While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC's policy rate at our December meeting. However, if inflation comes in substantially higher than I expect, more robust action by the FOMC may be called for. Let's just say it. September's inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining. Inflation based on personal consumption expenditures (PCE), the measure targeted by the FOMC, rose at a monthly rate of 0.5 percent in September and 3.7 percent over the previous 12 months. Core PCE inflation, excluding food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent in September and 3.1 percent from that time last year. Both these measures are too high, and I am particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases. Earlier this year, excessive inflation was driven by nonmarket prices that are estimated rather than observed by the government, and ones that I tend to discount as hard to measure and as an unreliable guide to the overall trend for core inflation. But now, two components with greater relevance to future inflation are elevated—core goods prices and those for core market-based services excluding housing. More than 70 percent of the components of core PCE service prices saw 12-month increases above 3 percent in September. Later today, I will be looking to see whether this breadth of elevated inflation continues, including whether high-tech goods prices related to the AI buildout continue to rise at the very high rate of recent months. I also want to know if the run-up in energy prices of the past several months is being passed through to goods and services directly or indirectly, because of higher input costs. While I am pleased to see energy prices down from their high rates over the past week or so, they are still quite elevated relative to the start of the year, and the ultimate effect on inflation will depend on what levels are sustained. Federal Reserve staff have been thinking hard about the effects on inflation of the AI buildout and elevated energy prices, and their findings do not encourage me to think that these factors will be fading anytime soon. In one exercise, researchers tried to capture imminent price pressures with a textual analysis of the well-known surveys of purchasing managers conducted by the Institute for Supply Management (ISM). 5 ISM surveys ask purchasing managers to list specific commodities, materials, and services whose prices rose or fell that month. 6 Staff used these responses to construct monthly price pressure indexes that correspond with actual categories of the producer price index (PPI). They found these indexes provide information about future changes in producer prices and, as a result, should have some signal about future PCE inflation. For example, the index for high-tech products rose in December 2025 and jumped further in January 2026, ahead of an escalation in those goods prices that eventually showed up in the February PPI and inflation data. The most recent ISM data, for October, point to the possibility of more price increases ahead. Some other Fed research indicates to me that energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past. 7 The researchers find a potential shift in the inflation process after the pandemic that suggests core inflation may be more responsive to energy shocks. Central bankers have tended to look through energy price shocks and expect that their effects on inflation will soon fade, but this new work cautions against taking too much comfort in this view. Their analysis suggests that, especially if oil prices were to remain elevated, these pressures could be larger than previously though and persist well into 2027. And there are reasons to also expect elevated energy prices to persist. First, even as there is increased tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, that traffic is moving at great expense. The insurance now needed for ships making this passing, and the ship-to-ship transfer of oil necessary to guard against Iranian attacks, are reportedly boosting oil prices by $20 to $30 a barrel. A second problem is that diesel oil production is affected by limited refining capacity and other constraints. As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East. To recap my economic outlook, economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above the FOMC's 2 percent goal. This means that even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting. That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text 2. See Christopher J. Waller (2026), "The Signaling Value of the Summary of Economic Projections," speech delivered at the Istanbul Economic Forum, Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, Istanbul, October 8. Return to text 3. Shakeena J. King and Daniela Mejía (2026), "Women Ages 65 and Over Now Make Up the Largest Share of Education Bachelor's Degree Holders," U.S. Census Bureau, America Counts: Stories Behind the Numbers, October 29. Return to text 4. The three-month moving average of workers reporting that they have been unemployed for 27 weeks or more increases from around 18 percent at the end of 2022 to more than 27 percent through September 2026. Return to text 5. Tomaz Cajner, Leland D. Crane, Christopher J. Kurz, Paul E. Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Press Releases Press Release November 09, 2026 Federal Reserve Board announces approval of two applications by Mutual Federal Bancorp, MHC, and MFB Bancorp, Inc. For release at 4:00 p.m. EST Share The Federal Reserve Board on Monday announced its approval of two applications by Mutual Federal Bancorp, MHC, and MFB Bancorp, Inc., both of Chicago, Illinois. These approvals allow the banking organization to have a new top-tier holding company, MFB Bancorp, Inc., which would become a savings and loan holding company by acquiring Mutual Federal Bank, of Chicago, Illinois. For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955. Order (PDF) Last Update:

title: AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)
body: AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026) Most of the cost of adopting something new isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist. The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines The new AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed. To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or update a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2 . V2 is available in 10 Regions , and committed baseline pricing is coming soon. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg – You can now migrate Parquet tables registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog into S3 Tables without building a pipeline or provisioning compute. S3 Tables validates the source and produces a compatibility report covering every object in scope. Each sync copies only what changed, so production keeps writing until cutover. Afterward you can query the table with Amazon Athena , Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio , or any engine that speaks the Iceberg REST API. You pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the conversion, and objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering keep their tier. At launch it works within the same account and Region, in 10 Regions. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written. Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize. AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode. AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday , Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge. AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub , with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS , and the new AgentCore Runtime. AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL. How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12). Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!
